content:
#Tau Ceti > PRs

I certainly don't.

(Given the current rate new PRs are made, it might be a good idea to make PR larger? Downside is how to ensure reviews remain just as through…)

Write the best [[small]], complete, sorry-free PR you can — optimised to pass the project's review rubrics.

Aim for [[~200–600 lines]] of genuine, non-vacuous content. A shorter PR that closes a milestone beats a longer peripheral one, and smaller-but-green beats bigger-but-broken.

Speaking of which, given how much money we're collectively burning on this, it may be a good idea to consider #Tau Ceti > Harness improvements? more carefully. A lot of the prompt sounds like inefficient prompt-engineering I think.

e.g.

Never write to the roadmaps.

If lake build is red, FIX IT or retreat (below). Never push red.

Read it in full; it is a few thousand tokens and the cheapest thing you will do this round.

Some discussions there:

#Autoformalization > Luna (!) only Trellis formulation of Bradač Ramsey paper
#Autoformalization > Efficient workflow?

(Easier said than done, I know. That needs work.)

Initially I thought frontier models along with their harness should have advanced agentic behaviors to handle PRs to Tau Ceti so that I only need to maintain extra care such as roadmap target selection, proof golfing and quality improvement prompts, and additional guardrails. But they deteriorate from time to time, and require human attention and intervention.

Later I moved to Tau Ceti worker loops, and started A/B testing, for some roadmaps I set up those additional care on top of worker loops, for some roadmaps I leave the raw worker running. For each roadmap, I have multiple (usually 4) "fronts" of worker loops, each focus on a "route" with 2 concurrent PRs.

From time to time, I check recent PRs on all fronts by agents and eyeballing, and repair PRs that are stuck, have quality issues, trapped in a review loop, turned a PR into trivial content after reviews, and exhausted fix attempt counts. During that process I would try to find the root cause and patch the worker (while avoiding AI over-engineering the patch), there are 53 PRs to my fork now. I also had been syncing from upstream and resolve conflicts by identifying intents from both sides and reconcile. (I have a light fork of Tau Ceti Review too, and my worker would refuse to review unless it has synced the latest upstream change so it won't drift or become stale.)

I also actively check PRs in batch, look for bad merges (sometimes reviewers gave a PR a pass with residual issues) and refactor opportunities then inject them so worker loops will pick them up and work on refactor PRs.

There is frequent agent stuck and significant token waste, and they need routine human attention. Some issues can be resolved by harness forks by contributors (and upstream can use agents to check forks to cherry-pick fixes), but some needs a mechanism to coorperatively stop rogue agents (e.g. stale reviewers, bad fixers).
to be fair “stale reviewer” shouldn't really count as “rogue agent” (I consider rogue to mean have a malicious intention), but either way the point stands.

my worker would refuse to review unless it has synced the latest upstream change so it won't drift or become stale

Sounds like a useful feature worth upstreaming, though it needs a human to review it (though one would need to think about how to implement it to still allow forks to function)
I skim or search it in sometimes. I recommend just muting the thread.
